\section{Background}
Phylogenetic inference assumes that sites in an alignment
share a common tree but may evolve at different rates.
The standard approach multiplies each site likelihood
by a rate drawn from a discretised gamma distribution,
which averages over rate variation without assigning rates to sites.

Site-strip models take a different view.
They partition the alignment into contiguous strips
and allow each strip its own rate multiplier,
so recombination breakpoints and structural boundaries
can be accommodated without changing the topology.

The idea is related to hidden Markov models along the alignment,
but the strip formulation keeps the number of parameters small
and makes posterior rates easy to interpret.

Early applications to viral genomes showed
that strip rates recover known recombination hotspots
and improve marginal likelihoods relative to the gamma model.

\section{Methods}
Our inference pipeline proceeds in three stages:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Align the sequences with a codon-aware aligner and trim unreliable columns.
\item Estimate the strip boundaries by a changepoint scan over site log-likelihoods.
\item Sample rates and topologies jointly with a Metropolis-coupled chain.
\section{Evaluation}
We simulate alignments under known strip structures
and measure how often the true boundaries are recovered.
Recovery is above ninety percent when strips are longer than two hundred sites,
and it degrades gracefully as strips shorten.

On empirical alignments the model selects between three and seven strips,
and the inferred boundaries align closely with annotated protein domains.

\section{Implementation}
The sampler is implemented as an extension of an open phylogenetics library
and runs on a single multicore workstation.
A typical analysis of forty taxa and twelve thousand sites
completes overnight with four coupled chains.
